blog-online.title: The Advantages of Online Bağlama Lessons
blocks: The bağlama, one of the most deeply rooted instruments of traditional music education, is being transformed by what the digital world has to offer. The greatest advantage of online bağlama lessons is, without doubt, that they remove geographical borders entirely. By bringing a master in the most remote corner of Anatolia and a student on the other side of the world into the same virtual classroom, this system builds a revolutionary bridge for passing on cultural heritage. After a busy working day, students can focus on their lessons in their own comfort zone, without physical obstacles such as traffic stress or travel fatigue. This not only saves time; by letting students practise where they are most at ease with their instrument—at home—it also minimises the psychological barriers in the learning process.

Another key advantage of the technology is fast access to visual and audio material. A small stroke of the plectrum (mızrap) or a finger position that can sometimes be missed in a traditional lesson can be examined in much greater detail online, thanks to high-resolution cameras and close-up shots. Interactive digital tools also let sheet music, exercise videos and backing recordings be shared in seconds, enriching the student’s practice routine. Learning isn’t limited to the weekly lesson either: because lessons can be recorded, students can rewatch every point where they got stuck and observe their own mistakes. This continuity helps technical skills settle into muscle memory much faster and stay there. Another essential element of online learning is the freedom to progress at your own pace. With no need to keep up with the general tempo of a classroom, students can spend as long as they like on a technique or a particular style (tavır) they find difficult. This personalised process keeps motivation high and the feeling of failure low.

On top of that, the backing tracks and the many metronome and rhythm patterns available digitally let students gain the experience of playing with an orchestra even when they practise alone. This modern approach turns the bağlama from a purely traditional instrument into an educational discipline that meets the needs of our time. In short, when combined with the right technological tools and a professional curriculum, online lessons turn learning the bağlama into a far more accessible, effective and sustainable journey. This harmony between academic knowledge and digital platforms opens a unique door of growth for the new generation of bağlama players—one without borders.

blog-baglama-secimi.title: What to Look for When Buying a Bağlama
blocks: A bağlama is an ocean steeped in the dust and soil of Anatolia, filtered through a thousand years of sorrow. When you pick it up, that piece of wood should whisper something to you. If you are going to buy a bağlama, let our first rule be this: the most expensive bağlama is not the best one. The best bağlama is the one that suits your hands, your voice and the style you want to play.
Don’t Rush It

When you walk into an instrument shop, don’t be dazzled by the over-polished bağlamas in the window, shining like mirrors under their polyester finish. That heavy varnish is often used as a “mask” to hide flaws in the wood or to keep unseasoned wood from cracking. What we care about is not the outside, but the soul beneath the soundboard.
The Lifeblood of the Wood: Seasoning

The first question to ask when buying a bağlama is: “How long has this wood been seasoned?” Leaving kiln-dried wood aside, we prefer wood that has dried and matured naturally. If the wood isn’t fully dry, three months after taking it home you’ll see the neck bend like a bow and the frets begin to buzz—a waste of your effort. Straight grain in the wood and close, parallel lines on the soundboard (the top) are the first signs of a mature instrument.
Choosing Style and Character

What style will you play? Will you follow the Neşet Ertaş school with the plectrum of the steppe, or are you after a more academic, “sparkling” tone like a TRT artist? If you are going to play in a traditional style (using the middle string, soft strokes), the depth of the body and the hardness of the wood should be chosen accordingly.
Remember: a master makes the bağlama, but it is your plectrum that turns it into a saz. We are looking for an instrument that speaks to the ear and the hand, not to the eye at first glance.
Part 1: Body Size, Shape and the “Carved or Staved?” Question

One of the things that will confuse you most when buying a bağlama is the famous question of centimetres. You’ll ask, “Teacher, should it be 38 or 42?” The answer actually lies in what you want to play.
Body Size and Tone
The general rule is this: the larger the body, the deeper (more bass) the sound; the smaller it is, the higher and clearer.

For the short neck (çöğür): Bodies of 38–40 cm are usually ideal. A size 39 body is easy to hold and gives that famous “bağlama tone” in a balanced way. If you try to make a 42–43 body into a short-neck instrument, the sound can be muffled and clumsy.

For the long neck (bozuk): Here bodies of 40 cm and above, especially 41–42 cm, are preferred. A large body is essential for the roaring sound of the long neck that sets semahs and bozlaks alight. But remember: the bigger the body, the more tiring it is physically. A saz that doesn’t sit well in your lap and makes your arm ache will soon end up as a wall decoration.
Staved or Carved?
This is where things get tricky.

Carved body: Our traditional, age-old method. It is made by hollowing out a single block of wood. The sound is fuller and more “focused”. Over the years, as the wood dries, the sound gets better; it is an heirloom instrument. But it is harder to look after: it reacts quickly to changes in temperature and is prone to cracking. A carved bağlama takes patience—it is delicate.

Staved body: Made by joining strips of wood together. Thanks to modern technology, wonderful staved instruments are made today. The sound projects more widely and has a “brighter” tone. It is less demanding to look after than a carved one. On professional stages and in studios, staved instruments are often preferred for their balanced sound.
Body Depth and Shape

Size alone isn’t enough; depth matters too. If the body is too deep, the sound gets trapped inside; if it is too shallow, it sounds tinny. The ideal is a golden ratio between length and depth. The shape of the back of the body also affects how it sits in your lap. Pointed bodies slip off your lap, while rounder shapes accompany you as if they were part of your body. When you hold the bağlama, the inside of your right elbow should rest comfortably on the highest point of the body. If your arm hangs in the air or bends too far down, that body is not the right size for you. The saz shouldn’t tire you out—you should be the one leading the saz.
Part 2: The Language of Wood—Which Wood, Which Sound?

Choosing the wood of a bağlama isn’t just about looks; the wood determines the instrument’s tone colour, its character and even its lifespan. The old masters used to say, “Look at the wood and hear its sound.” Every wood has its own frequency range.
1. Juniper: The “Burning” Voice of the Saz
If you play short neck and are looking for that soulful, burning, slightly rough yet full Anatolian tone, juniper is your remedy.
Character: Juniper projects the sound very quickly. Its mid and upper frequencies are very well balanced.

Who should buy it? It is the wood most often chosen for deyiş, nefes and the traditional bozlak style. Its grain is beautiful to look at, but its real gift is the distinctive “matte” texture of its sound.
2. Mulberry: The Sultan of the Saz
When people think of a traditional bağlama, mulberry is the first wood that comes to mind. It is the top choice for carved instruments in particular.

Character: Mulberry holds the sound in, lets it mature and only then releases it. The sound is very soft, with a “sweet” tone. Over the years, as the wood darkens, the sound becomes even more beautiful.

Note: When you first buy a mulberry saz, the sound may seem a little “closed”. But if you are patient and play it in, in a few years you’ll have a treasure in your hands. As the old saying goes, “a mulberry saz grows old together with its owner.”
3. Walnut: Balanced and Strong
Very widely used for both long and short necks. It is a hard, durable wood.
Character: Walnut has one of the best balances between bass and treble. Its sound is neither too burning nor too bright—right in the middle.
Who should buy it? If you want a single saz that does everything (both performance and recording), walnut is a good choice. Dark, closely grained pieces are especially prized.
4. Mahogany and Maple: Modern Tones
These woods have become very popular in staved instruments in recent years.
Mahogany: It has a reddish colour. The sound is very clean and smooth—tailor-made for studio recordings.
Maple: Usually light in colour. The sound is very bright and sharp. It helps the saz be heard even within a large orchestra.
Choosing the Soundboard

Whatever wood the body is made of, the thin board on top (the soundboard) is usually spruce. What to look for on the soundboard is lines that are very close together and perfectly straight. The closer those lines are, the better and more resilient the soundboard.
Part 3: Straightness, Thickness and Comfort of the Neck

The neck of the bağlama is the centre of both its physical durability and its playability. For a neck to be “good”, being made of quality wood isn’t enough; it must be worked properly and fit your hand.
1. Neck Material: Why Hornbeam?
The most popular wood for bağlama necks is hornbeam. The reason is that hornbeam is very hard and stable (it doesn’t warp easily).

Alternatives: You may also see mahogany or juniper necks. They look harmonious with the body, but they may not be as resilient as hornbeam. If you are looking for a professional instrument for life, go for a hornbeam neck with an ebony or rosewood fingerboard.
2. Neck Thickness: Made to Measure
One of the biggest mistakes is the prejudice that “a thin neck is better”. The thickness of the neck should be in proportion to the size of your palm and the length of your fingers.
A neck that is too thick: Makes it hard for your thumb to reach the upper strings (especially on the short neck) and tires your wrist quickly.

A neck that is too thin: It disappears in your hand while you play, makes it hard to get support when pressing down and—most dangerously—is more likely to bend forward over time under the tension of the strings.
The ideal: When you put your hand on the neck, your palm should grip it fully without squeezing.
3. Neck Straightness and Checking for Bowing
The first test to do when you pick up the saz is this: rest the body on your shoulder and look down the neck towards the pegs as if looking through a rifle scope.
The surface of the neck should run like a perfectly straight road.
If the neck twists to the left or right or curves upwards, stay away from that saz. Problems like these are usually defects that cannot be fixed or require expensive repairs.
4. Fingerboard and Fret Workmanship
A smooth fingerboard lets your fingers glide over the strings “like butter”.

Frets: The fret ties (nylon) should be neither so tight that they choke the wood nor so loose that they move. When you run your finger along the edges of the fingerboard, the ends of the frets shouldn’t scratch your hand. If they cut your hand, the workmanship is poor.
Ebony fingerboard: If you can, choose a saz with an ebony fingerboard. Because it is very hard, it doesn’t wear, and its jet-black, noble look gives the saz a completely different feel.

The neck is the backbone of the bağlama, my friend. A saz with a crooked backbone won’t speak true. When you try a saz, make sure the sound doesn’t buzz, especially on the frets near the middle. If a note doesn’t sound clean when you press a fret, either the neck is warped or the frets haven’t been levelled properly.

yapay-zeka.title: Artificial Intelligence in Music Education
blocks: Throughout history, music education has always been a matter of “transmission”. We used to sit at a master’s feet and watch for hours how he struck the plectrum and how he breathed. But the world has changed and time has sped up. Now we have a “Digital Master” that can analyse thousands of works in seconds, spot wrong notes instantly and draw up a practice plan just for us.
What Is Artificial Intelligence, and What Does It Do in Music?

What we call artificial intelligence is really the art of teaching computer software the human mind’s abilities to learn, analyse and synthesise. In music education it shows up in areas such as sound recognition, rhythm analysis, music notation and even stylistic composition. Imagine you are a bağlama student: we are talking about the luxury of an assistant who is always by your side to say, “Press that spot a bit more firmly,” when you strike the plectrum wrongly or don’t quite hit a koma note on the fret.
A Bridge Between Tradition and the Future

Many friends are worried: “Teacher, when the robots come, will our soul die?” No, my friend—the question isn’t whether the soul dies, but how we can cultivate that soul more effectively. AI is not coming to replace the music teacher, but to take the heavy, routine load off the teacher’s shoulders. When we hand over tasks like keeping the metronome, drilling basic scales and correcting simple wrong notes to AI, the teacher has time to convey the “feeling”, the “style” and the “story” of the music.
Data-Driven Learning

AI-supported platforms record on which day, at what time and in which passage a student gets stuck. For us educators, this data is priceless. We used to say “the student isn’t practising” and leave it at that; now we can say “the student is struggling with the syncopation in bar 17, which is why they get stuck there.” That is the first step towards personalised education.
Part 1: Tailor-Made Learning—How Algorithms Discover Talent

The biggest challenge in music education is “level”. Some students have a very sharp ear but clumsy fingers; others’ fingers fly like birds, but their sense of rhythm “limps” a little. In traditional teaching it is impossible for a teacher to spend 24 hours with each student and track these gaps one by one with millimetric precision. This is where AI comes in and works, so to speak, like an “X-ray machine”.
Everyone Has Their Own Rhythm

AI-supported learning platforms (for example, smart sheet-music readers or practice assistants) record every stroke of your plectrum and every breath. Even if you don’t notice, the algorithm will say: “Mahmut, you’re very good at even rhythms, but your right hand slows down a little in 5/8 aksak bars.” This is the student seeing their own reflection. AI adjusts the tempo to your pace. It slows down when you get stuck and raises the bar a notch as you improve. So it neither wears you out nor lets you stand still.
Real-Time Feedback: “Teacher, Am I Pressing It Right?”

In the past, if you memorised a piece wrongly, that mistake would “set in your bones” by the next lesson. Correcting it is harder than learning from scratch. Now there is AI watching you through your phone’s camera or microphone. The moment you press the wrong fret, a warning appears on the screen: “Careful, that note isn’t B, it’s B flat 2!” This immediate intervention stops mistakes from becoming habits. It helps students stay disciplined even when practising alone at home, as if “the teacher were there”.
A Curriculum Fed by Data

AI doesn’t just save the moment; it also plans the future. It analyses the techniques you are missing (for example trills or the “çekme” technique on the bağlama) and automatically adds exercises to fix them to your next practice list. In other words, it prepares a “tailor-made” curriculum for you. It does away with the question “What should I practise?” and says instead, “This is your weak spot—let’s fix it today.”
Motivation and Gamification

Boredom is the greatest enemy of music education. AI turns learning into a game. Imagine earning points for every note you play correctly and getting a medal when you pass a level. Our brains love this reward mechanism. Especially for younger students, it turns a dull lesson into an enjoyable journey.
Part 2: The Architect of Notes—Can AI Compose?

The highest step in music education is for students to find their own voice, that is, to compose. We used to hum for days and wear out our fingers on the neck of the bağlama to find a melody. Now we have an intelligence that, when we say “Write me a melody in the style of Neşet Ertaş but with a modern backing,” lays out options in seconds. So is this a miracle or an illusion?
1. Imitation or Creativity?

AI is essentially an enormous “probability calculator”. When you play it thousands of türküs, it learns which note is likely to follow which, and which makam evokes which emotion. So what it actually does is blend the heritage of the past and present it to us “as if it were new”. Can we call this “creativity” in the full sense? Perhaps not, but we can call it remarkable “technical craftsmanship”. In education it becomes a muse that tells students who are stuck, “Look, here’s another way.”
2. AI as a Composition Assistant

Music theory (harmony, counterpoint, makam theory) can sometimes be an intimidating wall for students. AI tears that wall down. You hum the main melody and it suggests suitable chords. You write a main theme and it offers variations on how it could be developed. This not only keeps students from drowning in theory but also broadens their horizons. It makes them say, “Oh, this chord suits this melody too!” In other words, AI doesn’t compose instead of you; it becomes your “co-creator”.
3. Algorithms and the Question of Makam and Style

The soul of our music lies in its koma notes and its distinctive “tavır” (style). AI has now begun to learn these microtonal structures too. When you ask an AI to “prepare a backing for an uzun hava in makam Hicaz”, it can lay a foundation that follows the rules of that makam. But here is the danger: if the student settles for what the AI offers, the result will be “perfect but soulless”. Because however much a machine learns, it cannot know the “sorrow”, the “longing” or the “rebellion” behind a türkü. It only offers a mathematical aesthetic made of ones and zeros.
4. The Birth of New Genres: Fusion and Experiments

AI is very skilled at combining the music of different cultures. It can take a bağlama melody and blend it with a synthetic sound never heard before. For a young person studying music, this means a limitless laboratory for building their own style. A new era is beginning in which genres blend and, when asked “what kind of music is this?”, the answer is “the shared cry of human and machine”.
Part 3: In Pursuit of Perfection—AI and Performance Analysis

To say a performance is “there”, knowing the notes isn’t enough; timing, dynamics and presence must also be right. Today AI opens a new horizon where a music teacher’s ears and eyes reach their limits. The era of “I think you were a bit out of tune” is over; the era of “your pitch drifted by 2%” has begun.
1. A Digital Mirror: Sound Analysis
AI-supported performance analysis tools examine your playing with millisecond precision. While you play a piece, the algorithm compares your sound with the original recording in the background.
Rhythm analysis: It shows you in visual graphs how far you deviated from the metronome. It tells you, “You rushed here, you dragged there.”

Intonation (clean pitch): Especially for fretless instruments, or for instruments like the bağlama with many koma notes, it checks whether you are pressing in exactly the right place. It measures the frequency of the note in hertz and guides you until you find the right pitch.
2. Image Processing: Posture and Technique
Hearing the sound isn’t enough—AI can now “see” us too. Through the computer’s camera it can analyse the position of your fingers, the angle of your wrist and even problems with how you sit.

Preventing a bad grip: Imagine an algorithm that tells you, “You’re bending your wrist too much—you’ll strain your tendons later.” Playing with the wrong technique can lead to lasting injuries or blocks in your playing. By tracking your skeletal movements, AI suggests the most ergonomic playing position.
3. Emotional Analysis: “Capturing the Soul”

Now you’ll say, “Teacher, what does a machine know about emotion?” You’re right—it doesn’t understand it, but it can measure imitated “emotional parameters”. Did you play the piece too harshly, or too lifelessly? By measuring how accurately you apply changes in volume—the “dynamics” (forte, piano)—it can score the expressive power of your performance. This is a step for students to stop being “robots that press notes” and begin adding their own interpretation.
4. Objective Assessment and Exam Anxiety

Teachers are human: they may be in a bad mood that day, overlook your mistake because they are fond of you, or be overly strict. But AI is objective. Holding exams under AI supervision gives a success score based entirely on data, beyond favouritism or personal opinion. And that brings fairness to education.
